Over on reddit, anemone has made another post detailing the next steps in his floathouse project...

While there are a few more details to the Maran floathouse that require nailing down, the design is fairly solid and I'm moving forward with a scale model at 1:12 scale, out of cheap materials, then we'll do a 1:4 scale model in actual geopolymer to prove out and learn some lessons about the slipforming process.

I know roughly how I want to do it. I'll take some stainless steel sheet metal, rivet extruded backing rails on them and use the rails as mounts to control the curvature of the sheet metal. Getting large sheets in the exact radius and also completely vertical is going to take some work, but the better it is the bigger the payoff. If concrete is going to slip vertically, acting like one big play-doh extruder, you can imagine it's important that the die doesn't become smaller near the bottom so as to bind the now solid concrete coming out. So the bottom portions should be somewhat more flexible.

I also think steel sheet-metal will be an okay material, but perhaps it would be wiser to use PTFE sheets inside there (basically teflon) to help it slip easier.

The other factor is that the larger you make the mold the faster you can slip the concrete. The concrete needs to be kept hot at 200° while it's slipping, so the slipform itself will be quite hot. We could use hot water for that, but blowing hot air or even internal heating elements might be better.

At the same time you have rebar going in from above both vertically and laterally off spools, and needs to be held fairly centered as it descends. We'll build comblike structures to facilitate the vertical drop. Once the bottom layers harden they'll hold in the bottom, then we keep the top straight and it will work from.

Then there's the top and bottom mold to worry about, these must be build from wood and nicely finished. They're reusable.

This all is going to take a number of people helping. The slipcast process must continue once it has started until finished. That means either some amount of hustle is needed to make it into a full day, or more than one shift is needed.

And again, longer and better build molds will shorten the amount of time, because it provides more hot length for the concrete to cure against, meaning you can slip faster and still have the material get a full 4 hours of heating.

And we can actually bring that heat level down considerably and compensate with a longer mold, which is probably a smart thing to do so people aren't constantly burning themselves on it. 200°F is really very hot, nearly boiling, and can sear flesh held against it, but if we bring the temp down to more like 170°--some people drink coffee at that temperature on the hot end. 140° is considered the "perfect drinking temperature" so that's probably the high end of hot coffee for most people, and you can put your hand on 140°F for several seconds no problem, maybe even hold it on there for awhile.

But that means a longer mold.

So you see, there are a lot of considerations here. If we build a 6' slipmold, that's 50% faster than a 4' slipmold. This material doesn't care how quickly we cast it.

When the time comes to begin building, I'll ask for volunteers. A lot of you have already volunteered and are on my mailing list for that day already.

Even after we begin building, I expect to keep production open and free to visit. I will train people in how to build them. You want to start building floathouses in India or Asia, come and learn, no problem. We'll make it a course, walk through the methods and learn.

All in good time.

For now, I've got a scale model to finish.

Tying work or value to some "unfakeable" resource is an essential step in avoiding Sybil attacks on these distributed projects.
